topic.title: Using surds and π in exact calculations
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M7 is two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. Exact answers are a Paper 1 speciality, and they sit in the last third of it. Four shapes recur across the papers read. Two or three marks for a length from Pythagoras with the instruction to give it as a surd, marked M1 then A1 for the square root and A1 for the simplified form (Summer 2021 M7 Paper 1 Q13, where the answer stayed as a single root). Two marks for a circle quantity in terms of π, usually a surface area or a perimeter, marked M1 A1 (Summer 2022 M7 Paper 2 Q11). Four marks for a perimeter that mixes a semicircle with a straight-sided shape, marked MA1 for the curved part, MA1 for the straight parts, MA1 for the equation and A1 for the exact answer (Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q12). Six marks at the very end of a paper for Pythagoras followed by an area, where the surd has to survive into the second step (November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q15, Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q12). The words that tell you to keep it exact are give your answer as a surd, in terms of π, or find the exact value.
mustMemorise: A surd is a root that will not come out exactly, so it is left under the root sign: √5 is a surd, √49 is not
√(k²n) = k√n — pull the largest square factor out, then root it
Area of a circle = πr², circumference = 2πr; neither is on the formula sheet
Perimeter of a semicircle = πr + 2r — the straight edge belongs to the shape
Exact means the root or the π stays in the answer: 5√2 and 25π are finished answers, 7.07 and 78.5 are not
π is a single number, so 3π + 4π = 7π and π × π would be π², not 2π
Pythagoras: a² + b² = c², and the exact length is whatever root comes out of it
notOnThisSpec: Rationalising a surd denominator — multiplying top and bottom by √n to clear a root from underneath. That is M8-NA-05, on the M8 papers only
Expanding brackets that contain surds, and conjugate pairs such as (3 + √2)(3 − √2) — also M8-NA-05
Proving that a number is rational or irrational, and deciding whether a recurring decimal is irrational — M8-NA-01
Adding and subtracting unlike surds as a topic in its own right; at M7 the surd arrives from one Pythagoras or one area and is simplified, not collected
Fractional indices as another way of writing a root, such as the one-half power of x — M8-NA-03
Radians, and any use of π as an angle measure — not on this specification at any tier

mustBeAbleTo: Say whether a root is a surd by testing it, rather than by looking for a root sign
Simplify a surd by finding its largest square factor and rooting that factor as it leaves the root sign
Use √a × √b = √(ab) and √a × √a = a, and square a whole surd term including its coefficient
Write the exact area and circumference of a circle in terms of π, from memory, from either the radius or the diameter
Work out the exact perimeter of a semicircle or a quarter circle, including every straight edge
Work out the exact area of a semicircle, a quarter circle and a shape with a circular piece removed

traps: Stopping at the root: the length is found, the square root is written down and the area or perimeter it was needed for is never worked out (November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q15, where the Pythagoras marks were common and the area defeated most)

workedExamples.stem:
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 6 cm and 3 cm.
Work out the length of the hypotenuse, giving your answer as a surd in its simplest form.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox="0 0 360 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><path d="M90 240 L246 240 L90 162 Z" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.07" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M90 226 L104 226 L104 240" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-size="13"><text x="168" y="262" text-anchor="middle">6 cm</text><text x="80" y="201" text-anchor="end">3 cm</text><text x="178" y="195">h</text></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-size="12.5"><text x="24" y="268">diagram not drawn accurately</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A right-angled triangle with the right angle at the bottom left. The horizontal side is labelled 6 cm, the vertical side is labelled 3 cm, and the sloping side is labelled h. A note reads: diagram not drawn accurately.

steps.decision: Pythagoras first, and nothing about the exact form changes it. The hypotenuse is the longest side, so the two known sides are squared and added.
45 is not a square number, so the root will not come out. That is the signal that this answer was always going to be a surd, and it is already worth a mark exactly as written.

options: Because 45 has no whole-number square root
Because the question said surd, so a root sign must appear somewhere
whyMenu.explain: The maths decides, not the wording. If the two sides had been 3 and 6 under root signs the answer would have come out whole, and a whole number would be the exact answer.

steps.decision: Hunt for the largest square factor. 9 is a square and 5 is left behind, so the 3 steps outside the root sign and the 5 stays in. Simplest form is what the last mark is for.

twin.stem:
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 2 cm and 8 cm.
Work out the hypotenuse, giving your answer as a surd in its simplest form.

workedExamples.stem:
A semicircle has radius 6 cm.
Work out its perimeter, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.

steps.working: Whole circle: $2\pi r = 2 \times \pi \times 6 = 12\pi$, so the curved edge is $\dfrac{12\pi}{2} = 6\pi$
steps.decision: Halve the circumference to get the curve. Doing the whole circle first and halving is safer than trying to remember a semicircle formula, and it leaves a line of working the scheme can credit.
Trace the outline with a finger: the flat edge is on the outside of the shape, so it counts. This is the line the examiners report as missing most often.

options: Because the diameter is part of the boundary of the shape
Because every perimeter has a straight part
Because the radius has to be used twice somewhere
whyMenu.explain: Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Cut a circle in half and you create a new edge, so that new edge has to be included.

steps.decision: The two parts are added and then left alone. $6\pi$ and 12 are not like terms, so nothing combines — and reaching for 30.85 here would give away the exact-form mark.

Work out its perimeter, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.

workedExamples.stem:
A circle of radius 5 cm is cut out of a square of side 10 cm, as shaded in the diagram.
Work out the exact area of the shaded region, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.

figure.alt: A square of side 10 cm with a circle of radius 5 cm drawn inside it, touching all four sides. The region between the circle and the square is shaded and labelled shaded. The radius is drawn and labelled 5 cm.

steps.decision: Shaded area means the big shape take away the hole, so both areas are needed separately before anything is subtracted.
Square the radius and leave $\pi$ in front. Only the 5 is squared: $\pi$ is a multiplier, not part of the base.
100 and $25\pi$ are unlike terms, so the subtraction cannot be carried out any further. An answer that looks unfinished can still be the finished exact answer.

options: Because 100 and $25\pi$ are not like terms
Because subtraction is not allowed in exact form
whyMenu.explain: Compare it with $100 - 25x$: nothing can be combined until you know what $x$ is. Here $x$ is $\pi$, and leaving it is the whole point. As a decimal the region measures about 21.46 cm².

workedExamples.stem:
In the parallelogram PQRS, $PQ = 9$ cm and $PS = 6$ cm. The perpendicular from S meets PQ at T, and $PT = 3$ cm.
Work out the exact area of the parallelogram, giving your answer in its simplest surd form.

figure.alt: A parallelogram PQRS with P at the bottom left and Q at the bottom right. A dashed perpendicular runs from S down to the point T on PQ, with a right-angle mark at T. PQ is labelled 9 cm, PS is labelled 6 cm, PT is labelled 3 cm and the dashed height is labelled h. A note reads: diagram not drawn accurately.

steps.working: Triangle PTS has a right angle at T, so $h^{2} = 6^{2} - 3^{2} = 36 - 9 = 27$
steps.decision: The height is not given, so it has to be built. PS is the hypotenuse of the little triangle because it faces the right angle, so this is a **subtraction**, not an addition.

options: Because PS is the hypotenuse, so its square is the total
Because the height is always smaller than the base
Because subtracting keeps the answer positive
whyMenu.explain: The hypotenuse squared equals the other two squares added, so finding one of the others means taking away. Adding here would give a height longer than the slant side, which the diagram forbids.

steps.decision: 9 is the largest square inside 27, so the 3 comes out. Simplify now, while the number is small — it keeps the multiplication in the next line easy.
This is the step the examiners report as the stumbling block. The surd behaves like a letter: 9 lots of 3 lots of $\sqrt{3}$ is $27\sqrt{3}$. The slant side 6 plays no part in the area.

twin.stem:
In a parallelogram the base is 10 cm and the slant side is 8 cm. The foot of the perpendicular from the top of the slant side is 4 cm along the base from its end.
Work out the exact area, in its simplest surd form.

items.stem: Which one of these is a surd?
items.skill: Tell a surd from a root that comes out exactly

options.feedback: $\sqrt{49} = 7$, so this root comes out exactly and is not a surd. Try the root before you judge it.
$50$ is not a square number, so this root has no exact decimal and has to keep its root sign. That is what makes it a surd.
$\sqrt{100} = 10$. A root sign on its own does not make a surd; the number underneath has to fail to come out.

items.stem: Which of these is $\sqrt{72}$ in its simplest surd form?
items.skill: Take the largest square factor out of a root

options.feedback: $72 = 36 \times 2$, and 36 is the largest square factor, so $6$ comes out and $2$ stays in.
The square factor 36 was taken outside without being rooted. It has to become $\sqrt{36} = 6$ as it leaves.
$72 = 6 \times 12$ is a true split, but 6 is not a square number, so nothing can come out of that root. Only a square factor may leave.

items.stem: A circle has radius 4 cm. What is its exact circumference?
items.skill: Choose between the circle formulae in exact form

options.feedback: $2\pi r = 2 \times \pi \times 4 = 8\pi$ cm. Leaving $\pi$ in is the whole answer.
$16\pi$ is $\pi r^{2}$, the **area** of this circle. Circumference is the distance once round, $2\pi r$.
That is the right length rounded. An exact-form question wants $\pi$ on the answer line, so $8\pi$ cm is the one that scores.

items.stem: A semicircle has radius 5 cm. What is its exact perimeter?
items.skill: Include the diameter in a semicircle perimeter

options.feedback: The curve is $\pi r = 5\pi$ and the straight edge is the diameter, 10 cm. Both are part of the boundary.
Only the curved edge was counted. Cutting the circle in half created a straight edge, and a perimeter goes all the way round.
$12.5\pi$ is the **area** of this semicircle, $\tfrac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}$. A perimeter is a distance round the edge.
A square root multiplied by itself gives back the number underneath, because that is exactly what a square root means.
The numbers under the roots were added. The rule multiplies them: $\sqrt{5} \times \sqrt{5} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
The root sign has been kept when it should have gone. $\sqrt{25}$ is exactly 5, so no root survives.

items.skill: Square a whole surd term, coefficient and all

options.feedback: Both parts are squared: $3^{2} \times (\sqrt{2})^{2} = 9 \times 2 = 18$.
Only the root was squared; the 3 in front was left as it was. Squaring a product squares every factor in it.
Only the 3 was squared; the root was carried down untouched. $(\sqrt{2})^{2}$ is 2, so the root disappears.

items.stem: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and perpendicular height $3\sqrt{5}$ cm. What is its exact area?
items.skill: Carry a surd into an area calculation

options.feedback: Base times perpendicular height: $8 \times 3\sqrt{5} = 24\sqrt{5}$ cm². The root is simply carried along.
The two lengths were added rather than multiplied. Area needs base times height, and the surd multiplies like any other factor.
That is the right area rounded. Exact form keeps the root: $24\sqrt{5}$ cm².

items.stem: A question asks for the area of a circle of radius 5 cm **in terms of $\pi$**. Which answer takes the mark?
items.skill: Recognise which form an exact-answer instruction demands

options.feedback: $\pi \times 5^{2} = 25\pi$ cm². The instruction was to keep $\pi$, and this one does.
The value is right and the form is not. A decimal is a rounded copy, and the last mark on these questions is for the exact form.
3.14 is an approximation of $\pi$, not $\pi$ itself, so this stops being exact as soon as it is written.

parts.stem: Simplify $\sqrt{8}$, giving your answer in its simplest surd form.
hints: Look for the largest square number that divides 8.
4 is a square number, and 8 divided by 4 is 2.
parts.workedSolution:
$8 = 4 \times 2$, and 4 is a square number.
$\sqrt{8} = \sqrt{4} \times \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}$.
Check: $2^{2} \times 2 = 8$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square factor 4 was carried outside the root sign without being rooted. It has to become $\sqrt{4} = 2$ on the way out, which gives $2\sqrt{2}$.
The size is right, but the question asked for surd form. Write $2\sqrt{2}$ on the answer line; the decimal is a rounded copy and cannot take the mark.

$\sqrt{75} = \sqrt{25} \times \sqrt{3} = 5\sqrt{3}$.

$A = \pi r^{2} = \pi \times 3^{2} = 9\pi$ cm².

$A = \pi r^{2} = \pi \times 7^{2} = 49\pi$ cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The diameter was used where the radius belongs, so the area came out four times too big. Halve the 14 cm first, then square.

parts.stem:
A semicircle has radius 8 cm.
Work out its perimeter, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hints: Halve the circumference of the whole circle for the curve.
Then look at the straight edge along the bottom.
parts.workedSolution:
Curve: half of $2\pi \times 8 = 16\pi$, which is $8\pi$ cm.
Straight edge: the diameter, $2 \times 8 = 16$ cm.
Perimeter $= 8\pi + 16$ cm, which is about 41.13 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The curve is right and the flat edge was left out. Cutting a circle in half creates a new straight edge, and it belongs to the perimeter: add $16$.
$32\pi$ is the area of this semicircle. A perimeter is a distance round the edge, so it needs the arc and the diameter instead.

parts.stem:
A semicircle has radius 8 cm.

hints: Find the whole circle first.
Then halve it.
parts.workedSolution:
Whole circle: $\pi \times 8^{2} = 64\pi$ cm².
Half of that is $32\pi$ cm².

commonErrors.feedback: $8\pi$ is the curved **length** of this semicircle. Area needs $\pi r^{2}$ halved, which gives $32\pi$ cm².
The size is right. The form is not: leave $\pi$ in and write $32\pi$ cm².

parts.stem: Work out the exact value of $\sqrt{12} \times \sqrt{3}$.
hints: Two roots multiplied become one root over the product.
parts.workedSolution:
$\sqrt{12} \times \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{12 \times 3} = \sqrt{36} = 6$.
The surds vanished because 36 is a square number. Not every surd calculation ends with a root sign.

commonErrors.feedback: The numbers under the roots were added rather than multiplied. $\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$, so this one is $\sqrt{36}$.

parts.stem:
The diagonal of a square is 6 cm.
Show that the exact area of the square is 18 cm².

rubric: Pythagoras written with the two equal sides: $x^{2} + x^{2} = 6^{2}$
area $= x^{2} = 18$ cm² stated, with the diagonal never rounded

hints: The diagonal cuts the square into two right-angled triangles.
Call the side $x$. Both shorter sides of the triangle are $x$.
The area is $x^{2}$, and you have just found $x^{2}$ without needing $x$.
parts.workedSolution:
Let the side be $x$ cm. The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with two sides of $x$:
$x^{2} + x^{2} = 6^{2}$, so $2x^{2} = 36$ and $x^{2} = 18$.
The area of the square is $x^{2}$, so the area is 18 cm² exactly.
You never needed $x$ itself. If you do want it, $x = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$ cm, and squaring that gives 18 again.

commonErrors.feedback: The side was rounded to a decimal before being squared, so the 18 arrives only approximately. Keep $x^{2} = 18$ and the result is exact in one line.

parts.stem:
A quarter circle has radius 6 cm.
Work out its perimeter, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hints: A quarter circle has one curved edge and two straight ones.
Both straight edges are radii.
parts.workedSolution:
Curve: a quarter of $2\pi \times 6 = 12\pi$, which is $3\pi$ cm.
Straight edges: two radii, $6 + 6 = 12$ cm.
Perimeter $= 3\pi + 12$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the curve was counted. The two radii are edges of the shape as well, so 12 has to be added.
That is the **area** of the quarter circle. The perimeter is a distance: one arc and two radii.

parts.stem:
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of $\sqrt{3}$ cm and $\sqrt{6}$ cm.
Work out the exact length of the hypotenuse.
hints: Squaring a root undoes it.
So the two squares are just 3 and 6.
parts.workedSolution:
$h^{2} = (\sqrt{3})^{2} + (\sqrt{6})^{2} = 3 + 6 = 9$.
$h = \sqrt{9} = 3$ cm.
Both roots disappeared the moment they were squared, and the exact answer turned out to be a whole number.

commonErrors.feedback: $\sqrt{9}$ is the right value, and 9 is a square number, so finish it: the exact answer is 3 cm.
The two sides were multiplied rather than squared and added. Pythagoras squares each side first, and squaring $\sqrt{3}$ simply gives 3.

parts.stem:
A metal plate is a rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm with a semicircle pressed out of one end. The semicircle has the 6 cm side as its diameter.
Work out the exact area of the plate, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hints: Find the rectangle, then the piece taken away.
The semicircle's radius is half of 6.
parts.workedSolution:
Rectangle: $10 \times 6 = 60$ cm².
Semicircle: radius $= 6 \div 2 = 3$ cm, so its area is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 3^{2} = 4.5\pi$ cm².
Plate: $60 - 4.5\pi$ cm², which is about 45.86 cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The 6 cm was used as the radius. It is the diameter, so halve it to 3 cm before squaring.
That is the area rounded. The question asked for exact form, so leave it as $60 - 4.5\pi$ cm². The method mark is safe.

parts.stem: Work out the exact perimeter of the plate, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hints: Trace right round the outside and name each edge as you pass it.
The 6 cm edge at the curved end is no longer there — the curve replaced it.
parts.workedSolution:
Going round: 10 cm along the top, 10 cm along the bottom, 6 cm up the straight end, and then the curve.
Straight parts: $10 + 10 + 6 = 26$ cm.
Curve: half of $2\pi \times 3$, which is $3\pi$ cm.
Perimeter $= 26 + 3\pi$ cm, about 35.42 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The 6 cm end was counted at both ends of the plate. At the curved end that edge has been replaced by the arc, so it is not part of the boundary any more.
The semicircle's area has been added to a set of lengths. Only the curved **length**, $3\pi$ cm, belongs in a perimeter.

parts.stem:
A triangular sail is isosceles. Its two equal sides are 7 m and its base is 6 m.
Find the perpendicular height of the sail, giving your answer as a surd in its simplest form.

scheme.for: $7^{2} - 3^{2}$ seen, with 3 as half the base

hints: The perpendicular from the top splits the base into two equal halves.
That makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 3.
parts.workedSolution:
The perpendicular cuts the base in half, so the right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 7 m and one shorter side 3 m.
$h^{2} = 7^{2} - 3^{2} = 49 - 9 = 40$.
$h = \sqrt{40} = \sqrt{4} \times \sqrt{10} = 2\sqrt{10}$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole base was used instead of half of it. The perpendicular meets the base at its midpoint, so the shorter side of the right-angled triangle is 3 m.
Right height, wrong form, and part (b) will need the exact version anyway. Write $2\sqrt{10}$ m.

parts.stem: Hence find the exact area of the sail, giving your answer as a surd in its simplest form.
hints: Area of a triangle is half the base times the perpendicular height.
The surd multiplies like a letter: keep the root and work on the numbers in front.
parts.workedSolution:
Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 2\sqrt{10} = 3 \times 2\sqrt{10} = 6\sqrt{10}$ m².
About 18.97 m² as a decimal, but the exact form is what is asked for. The 7 m sides play no part in the area.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the height from part (a), not the area. Multiply it by half the base to finish: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 2\sqrt{10} = 6\sqrt{10}$ m².
Base times height is the area of a **parallelogram**. A triangle takes half of that, so halve it once more.

parts.stem:
A square paving slab has an area of 32 cm².
Work out its perimeter, giving your answer as a surd in its simplest form.
You must show your working.
hints: Area of a square is side squared, so the side is the square root of the area.
Simplify the root before multiplying by 4.
32 has a large square factor.
parts.workedSolution:
Side $= \sqrt{32}$ cm.
$32 = 16 \times 2$, so the side is $4\sqrt{2}$ cm.
Perimeter $= 4 \times 4\sqrt{2} = 16\sqrt{2}$ cm, which is about 22.63 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The square factor 16 left the root sign without being rooted. $\sqrt{16} = 4$, so the side is $4\sqrt{2}$ cm and the perimeter is $16\sqrt{2}$ cm.
That is the side, and the question asked for the perimeter. Four equal sides: multiply by 4 to reach $16\sqrt{2}$ cm.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

context.setting: A circular badge given by its circumference

parts.stem:
A circular badge has a circumference of $12\pi$ cm.
Work out its area, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
You must show your working.
hints: Put the circumference into $2\pi r$ and solve for $r$.
The $\pi$ on each side cancels, which is why no calculator is needed.
Then use $\pi r^{2}$.
parts.workedSolution:
$2\pi r = 12\pi$.
Divide both sides by $2\pi$: $r = \dfrac{12\pi}{2\pi} = 6$ cm. The $\pi$ cancels because it sits on both sides.
Area $= \pi r^{2} = \pi \times 6^{2} = 36\pi$ cm², about 113.1 cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The 12 from $12\pi$ was treated as the radius. It is the circumference divided by $\pi$, which is the **diameter**; the radius is 6 cm.
The area is right and the form is not. With no calculator, $36\pi$ cm² is also far quicker to write.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked: a semicircle has radius 7 cm. Work out its perimeter, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. Her working:
studentWorking: Circumference of whole circle = 2 x pi x 7 = 14pi
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are correct and would earn the method mark. Line 3 calls the curved edge the whole perimeter. Slicing a circle in half creates a new straight edge — the diameter — and a perimeter is the distance all the way round the boundary, so that 14 cm belongs in the answer.
findTheMistake.feedback: The circle work is sound, and on a question about the arc alone it would have scored everything. Examiners named this exact omission on the Summer 2023 semicircle question. One habit fixes it: draw the shape and trace its outline with your pencil before you write, saying each edge out loud as you pass it. The answer is 21.99 cm the wrong way and 35.99 cm the right way, so a rough size check catches it too.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked: a circle has radius 4 cm. Work out its area, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is the right formula. Line 2 swaps $\pi$ for 3.14, and from that point on the answer is an approximation. The true value is 50.2655..., so 50.24 is not even correct to two decimal places, and in terms of $\pi$ means $\pi$ must still be visible on the answer line.
findTheMistake.feedback: The formula and the squaring were both right, so the method mark stands. Examiners reported this substitution on the Summer 2023 semicircle question, where it cost the final mark. On Paper 1 the exact form is also the easier one: $16\pi$ takes one line and no long multiplication.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara was asked to simplify $\sqrt{48}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are exactly the right thinking: the largest square factor of 48 is 16. Line 3 moves that 16 outside the root sign unchanged. A factor that leaves a square root has to be rooted on the way out, so it becomes $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The factor hunt was the hard part and it was done well. One check catches the slip every time: square your answer back. $16\sqrt{3}$ is about 27.71, far above $\sqrt{48} \approx 6.93$, while $4\sqrt{3}$ squares back to 48 exactly.

prompts.prompt: What makes a number a surd?
prompts.answer: It is a root that cannot be written exactly as a whole number or a fraction, so it is left under the root sign. $\sqrt{5}$ is a surd; $\sqrt{49}$ is not, because it is 7.

prompts.prompt: How do you simplify a surd such as $\sqrt{72}$?
prompts.answer: Find the largest square factor, split the root in two and root only the square part: $72 = 36 \times 2$, so $\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}$.

prompts.prompt: Write down the area and the circumference of a circle of radius $r$ in exact form.
prompts.answer: Area $= \pi r^{2}$ and circumference $= 2\pi r$. Neither is on the M7 formula sheet, so both must be known.

prompts.prompt: What is the perimeter of a semicircle of radius $r$?
prompts.answer: $\pi r + 2r$. The curved edge is half the circumference and the straight edge is the diameter, and both are part of the boundary.

prompts.prompt: What is the area of a semicircle of radius $r$?
prompts.answer: $\tfrac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}$ — the area of the whole circle, halved.

prompts.prompt: A question says **give your answer in terms of $\pi$**. What must the answer line show?
prompts.answer: $\pi$ itself, still written as $\pi$. No 3.14, no decimal, no rounded value — those are approximations and the final mark is for the exact form.
$a$, and $\sqrt{ab}$. Multiplying two roots multiplies what is underneath; multiplying a root by itself removes the root sign altogether.

prompts.prompt: How do you get an exact length out of Pythagoras?
prompts.answer: Square the two known sides, add for a hypotenuse or subtract for a shorter side, then take the square root and simplify it. Do not reach for a decimal at any point.

prompts.prompt: Someone writes $\sqrt{50} = 25\sqrt{2}$. What went wrong, and what is the right answer?
prompts.answer: The square factor 25 was carried outside the root sign without being rooted. It has to become $\sqrt{25} = 5$ on the way out, so $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$.

prompts.prompt: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height $3\sqrt{5}$ cm. What is its exact area?
prompts.answer: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 3\sqrt{5} = 12\sqrt{5}$ cm². The surd multiplies like a letter; only the numbers in front change.

findings.asked: Pythagoras for one length, then the perimeter of a semicircle in terms of pi, for four marks.
findings.wentWrong: Many reached the surd for one mark and went no further. The diameter was left out of the semicircle perimeter, the area formula was used where a perimeter was wanted, and 3.14 replaced pi so the answer stopped being exact. The unit overview named the question as beyond most of the entry.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Added the arc and the diameter, and kept pi in the answer to the last line.
findings.rule: Trace the outline first, then keep pi.

findings.asked: Pythagoras, surds and areas together in one problem that was not broken into steps.
findings.wentWrong: The question separated the entry. Most made a start, but only the strongest carried the exact length through the later steps; squaring a surd term was where several came apart.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the length as a surd and used it, unrounded, inside the area that followed.
findings.rule: Square the whole term, coefficient and root together.

findings.asked: Pythagoras and then the area of a parallelogram, in exact form, as the final six-mark question.
findings.wentWrong: Most earned the two marks for the Pythagoras step. The area was reported as the stumbling block, and only the strongest tenth of the entry finished the question.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Multiplied base by the surd height and left the root in the answer.
findings.rule: The exact length is a means, not the answer.

insight.ruleToRemember: Exact means exact: a root stays a root and pi stays pi, all the way to the answer line. Simplify the root by pulling out the largest square factor, rooting it as it leaves, and then carry that surd into whatever the question actually asked for.
insight.aStarSignal: Finding a length as a surd and using it, unrounded and unsimplified into a decimal, inside the area or perimeter that follows.
